title: Early Stopping as a Privacy Mechanism: Exploiting the Generalization-Memorization Gap in Diffusion Models for Differentially Private Generation
description: Problem: Existing differentially private (DP) training for diffusion models relies on DP-SGD, which adds calibrated noise to gradients and significantly degrades sample quality. The anchor paper reveals that memorization only emerges after a training time τ_mem that grows linearly with dataset size n, while generalization begins at a constant τ_gen. This creates an exploitable window where models generalize without memorizing — suggesting early stopping alone may provide meaningful privacy guarantees without gradient noise. Proposed Method: We formalize early stopping as a privacy mechanism by (1) deriving Rényi differential privacy bounds for diffusion models stopped at time τ < τ_mem using empirical memorization metrics (e.g., extractable training examples), (2) proposing an adaptive stopping criterion that monitors memorization onset via per-sample loss trajectories, and (3) combining early stopping with lightweight DP-SGD (reduced noise multiplier) to achieve better utility-privacy tradeoffs. Planned Experiments: We train DDPM/EDM models on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and MIMIC-CXR (medical imaging) with varying n, measuring privacy via membership inference attacks and extraction rates at different stopping times. We compare FID/precision-recall against full DP-SGD baselines, and validate that τ_mem scaling with n predicts empirically measured privacy leakage, establishing early stopping as a principled, cheap privacy technique for data-limited domains like medical imaging.

Specifically, we track: (1) the evolution of score function Jacobian norms on a held-out probe set, which we hypothesize sharpens near memorization onset; (2) nearest-neighbor distances in denoised latent space between generated and training samples across noise levels; and (3) per-sample loss variance statistics. Existing checkpointing strategies rely on fixed schedules or heuristic validation losses that don't directly measure memorization onset.

Proposed Method: We develop an online memorization detection criterion that monitors training dynamics to adaptively identify τ_mem without requiring held-out test sets. Specifically, we propose tracking the divergence between the learned score function's behavior on training samples versus slightly perturbed neighbors (using k-NN distances in activation space). As memorization emerges, this divergence should sharply increase. We formalize this as a 'memorization score' computed cheaply during training, and use it to trigger early stopping or switch to a regularized fine-tuning phase. We also propose a lightweight linear-scaling rule: estimate τ_mem ≈ c·n from a small pilot run, then extrapolate to full dataset size.

Experiments: (1) Validate memorization score against ground-truth τ_mem on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and medical imaging datasets with varying n. (2) Compare adaptive stopping against fixed-schedule baselines on FID, memorization rate (via nearest-neighbor retrieval), and privacy metrics. (3) Test extrapolation accuracy of the linear-scaling rule across dataset sizes. (4) Evaluate on text-to-image diffusion models (Stable Diffusion fine-tuning) to test scalability.

title: Adaptive Early Stopping via Online Memorization Detection for Diffusion Models
description: Problem: The anchor paper identifies a critical training window [τ_gen, τ_mem] where diffusion models generalize without memorizing, and shows τ_mem scales linearly with dataset size n. However, practitioners currently lack efficient, online methods to detect when a model is approaching τ_mem during training, forcing either expensive post-hoc audits or conservative fixed-step stopping rules that sacrifice sample quality. Proposed Method: We develop a lightweight online memorization detector that runs concurrently with training. At each checkpoint, we compute a memorization score using a small held-out 'canary' subset — carefully constructed synthetic near-duplicates of training samples — and track the trajectory of their denoising loss relative to genuine training samples. When this ratio crosses a learned threshold (calibrated via the theoretical τ_mem ∝ n relationship), training is halted. We additionally propose an adaptive learning rate schedule that slows training as memorization risk increases, extending the generalization window without sacrificing convergence. Experiments: (1) Validate detector accuracy on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and medical imaging datasets across dataset sizes; (2) Compare sample quality (FID, precision/recall) versus fixed-step stopping baselines; (3) Measure privacy risk using membership inference attacks at stopping points; (4) Ablate canary construction strategies and threshold calibration methods; (5) Test on latent diffusion models to verify scalability.

title: Adaptive Early Stopping for Diffusion Models via Online Memorization Detection
description: Problem: The anchor paper identifies a critical training window [τ_gen, τ_mem] where diffusion models generalize well, with τ_mem scaling linearly with dataset size n. However, practitioners currently lack principled, computationally cheap criteria to detect when a model is approaching τ_mem during training, forcing either conservative under-training or expensive post-hoc auditing for memorization. Proposed Method: We develop an online memorization detection framework that monitors lightweight proxy signals during training to estimate τ_mem in real-time. Specifically, we propose three complementary indicators: (1) a gradient alignment score measuring convergence of per-sample gradients toward individual training examples, (2) a nearest-neighbor divergence metric in the diffusion model's intermediate feature space comparing generated samples to training data, and (3) a memorization-sensitive EMA of the training loss curvature. We combine these into an adaptive early stopping criterion that halts training just before τ_mem, automatically calibrated to dataset size. Experiments: We validate on CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, and ImageNet at varying dataset sizes (1K–500K samples), measuring FID, memorization rate (via SSCD similarity), and stopping accuracy relative to ground-truth τ_mem. We compare against fixed-epoch baselines, standard early stopping heuristics, and ablations of each signal component, demonstrating improved generalization-memorization tradeoff with 20-40% reduced training compute.

title: Adaptive Training Termination for Diffusion Models via Online Memorization Detection
description:
Problem: The anchor paper identifies a critical window [τ_gen, τ_mem] during diffusion model training where generalization occurs, with τ_mem scaling linearly with dataset size n. However, practitioners currently lack principled stopping criteria to exploit this window—they either overtrain (causing memorization) or undertrain (sacrificing quality). This is especially problematic for small datasets in medical imaging, drug discovery, or personalized generation.

Proposed Method: We develop an online memorization detection algorithm that monitors training dynamics in real-time to automatically halt training near τ_mem. Our approach tracks two lightweight signals: (1) a nearest-neighbor memorization score computed on a held-out probe set by measuring whether generated samples collapse toward training examples in feature space, and (2) the variance of denoising scores across training samples as a proxy for memorization onset. We combine these into an adaptive early stopping criterion with theoretical guarantees based on the linear scaling of τ_mem with n. We further propose a curriculum that dynamically adjusts noise schedules to extend the generalization window.

Experiments: We validate on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and medical imaging datasets (ChestX-ray14) at varying dataset sizes. Metrics include FID, memorization rate (extraction attacks), and privacy risk scores. We compare against standard early stopping, differential privacy baselines, and demonstrate that our method achieves near-optimal quality-privacy tradeoffs without privacy budget overhead.
